newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland paras escaped murder charge - Irish expert.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland paras escaped murder charge - Irish expert.

text.p: An Irish legal expert said on Thursday that some of the British paratroopers involved in the "Bloody Sunday" killings in Northern Ireland in 1972 should have been prosecuted for murder.
Dermot Walsh, a law professor at Limerick University, was speaking on the 25th anniversary of the shooting of 13 unarmed Roman Catholic Irish nationalists in Londonderry city.

He told Reuters there were discrepancies in the statements made by the soldiers to a British enquiry into the killings. Britain released the statements last year under pressure from victims' relatives and a human rights group, he said.
"There are grounds for preferring charges of murder or attempted murder against some of the soldiers on the basis of some of their original statements," he said.
Walsh was speaking ahead of publication in Londonderry of his critical study of the official report by Lord Widgery, who was then Britain's chief justice.
"The Widgery findings are fatally flawed because they are based substantially on unreliable evidence," he said.
Widgery said the troops had been fired on and that some of the dead might have handled weapons or explosives before they were hit.

Northern Ireland's minority Catholics, who generally favour uniting the province with the Irish republic, regard the report as a "whitewash" of what they say were unprovoked killings at an Irish nationalist rally.
No soldiers were hurt and no weapons were found at the scene of the killings, in the heart of Londonderry's Bogside district.
Walsh examined papers, including soldiers' "original statements", which he said conflicted materially with evidence they gave to the Widgery tribunal.
"These new documents...contain original statements that soldiers gave on the night of Bloody Sunday to military police, and in addition a lot of other things such as memos," he said.
It was disturbing, he said, that "the soldiers' original statements were available to counsel for the tribunal and Lord Widgery but not counsel for the deceased".
"The whole report was seriously infected by the appearance of a bias to the extent that it undermined its whole legality," the Irish professor said.
"Most disturbing of all is the fact that (the documents) portray Lord Widgery himself as being prepared to play down evidence favourable to the deceased and amplify evidence favourable to the Army."
Bells will toll in churches in predominantly Roman Catholic Londonderry and local people will observe two minutes silence at 16.30 GMT marking the time the 20-minute hail of gunfire stopped.
Support for relatives' demands for a new inquiry has come from the Irish government with which Northern Ireland's Catholic minority closely identifies.

"We understand the strong feelings of the families concerned and the belief that the reputations of their loved ones have not been vindicated in the appropriate way," Prime Minister John Bruton told parliament in Dublin this week.

Londonderry legislator John Hume, leader of the moderate Catholic Social Democratic and Labour Party, and more than 60 other members of the British parliament on Wednesday also called for a new investigation.
But the British government says it has no plans for one.
"Bloody Sunday" is widely regarded as a milestone that marked a rapid deterioration in the province's security climate.

It intensified the Catholic minority's distrust of British rule. Disaffected youths swelled the ranks of the Irish Republican Army, a guerrilla force that continues to wage a war for a united Ireland.
